Why Democrat Scott Colom’s Senate win in Mississippi is so significant

Democrat Scott Colom has won the US Senate race in Mississippi, delivering a shock victory for the party in a deeply conservative state that has elected Republicans for decades.

Colom's victory makes him the first black person from Mississippi to be seated in the US Senate since Blanche Bruce served from 1875 to 1881.

Fewer than five thousand votes out of nearly a million counted separated him from his Republican opponent, the incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith.

The result means the Democrats will hold 55 seats in the 100-member Senate, with a knife-edge race in Alaska still to be called.

Before Scott Colom, these two men were the last black US senators in Mississippi

Colom, 43, won with 49.2% of the vote. Hyde-Smith, who received 48.7%, congratulated Colom in a video posted on X on Wednesday evening and wished him well.

"While this was not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters," she said.

The contest was not considered to be in play until the final weeks of the campaign, given President Donald Trump won the state in the 2024 election by more than 22 points.

Colom offered a victory speech on the campus of Tougaloo College, met by hundreds of cheering supporters standing side-by-side under the night sky.

A crowd of supporters turned out to cheer Colom's win

Excitement filled the air as he thanked them for the support over the days of waiting for a result since the 4 November election.

"They did not believe a moment like this was possible, but I kept the faith," Colom said.

"It's not something that I did y'all," he continued. "It's something we did."

"In Mississippi, it's local people that make the difference."

Dozens of people were gathered at the Mississippi HQ of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP) in Jackson on Wednesday when Colom's victory was announced.

The room burst into deafening applause and cheers.

"This is an amazing result," said Leon Russell, chairman of the NAACP board.

"This is purely the work of particularly the black community," he continued. "There was not a whole lot of money, but there was a whole lot of organising.

Across the room, filled with people embracing, Amber Thomas sat, revelling in the victory.

"When you fight, you win," Thomas said. "Right now, I am overwhelmed with joy."

Colom supporters celebrate his win in Jackson, Mississippi

The last black senator in the state before Colom was Bruce who was chosen by the state legislature.

It has taken a century and a half for the state to choose a new one, this time by Mississippi voters.

In his campaign, Colom strove to engage Republican voters, even going to a Trump rally to speak to people in line outside.

Another key moment was his opponent telling voters to "pick another protein" when asked about surging beef prices, something Colom turned into a viral advert of his own. , external

Republican Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith has been in the Senate since 2018

Colom appeared to a ride a national wave of resentment against Republicans.

Voter backlash against Trump's Republican party has been driven in large part by economic woes, blamed on his administration's tariffs and war with Iran, according to exit polls.

Colom, a local prosecutor, used the national mood to his advantage, highlighting his opponent's support for Trump's tariffs and giving her the nickname "Cindy High Prices".

The Democrat campaigned aggressively, visiting all of Mississippi's 82 counties.

Hyde-Smith's campaign assailed Colom as a puppet of billionaire liberal donor George Soros, whose family has helped fund the Democrat's political campaigns.

The 67-year-old Republican was criticised for a lack of public appearances.

Democrats have scored a series of major wins in these midterm elections, taking control of both the US House of Representatives and the Senate.

The party flipped Senate seats in Republican strongholds, including Texas, South Carolina, Kansas and Iowa.

Alan Milburn will publish his review next week

Some young people could see reductions to the benefits they are entitled to under a radical overhaul of the welfare system to be recommended by a government-commissioned review.

As reported in the Times, , external Alan Milburn's year-long report, to be published on Tuesday, is expected to recommend moving under-25s off the main sickness and disability benefits.

Milburn, a former Labour health secretary, has been tasked by the government with helping reduce the one in eight 16 to 24 year-olds in the UK who are not in education, employment or training - otherwise known as "Neet".

He said on Wednesday night that his plans would not be "pain-free" and would affect both existing and new claimants.

His report is expected to say that under-25s should no longer be able to claim the health element of UK-wide universal credit - or personal independence payment (Pip), the main disability benefit in England and Wales.

Disabled people in Scotland can claim the devolved Adult Disability Payment.

Instead, under Milburn's plan, under-25s would receive an allowance on the same basic rate as universal credit.

Some could be eligible for a new "additional cost allowance" to cover day-to-day costs related to their conditions.

Some claimants would receive less under the plans - although the exact amounts will not be clear until early next year, when the government publishes legislation to implement the changes.

People can claim Pip to help them with the additional cost of being disabled or living with long-term physical or mental health conditions. It is available to those both in and out of work.

In his interim report, , external Milburn said survey data found that 19% of young people claiming disability or health benefits were in work.

Milburn, a Labour MP from 1992 to 2010, is also expected to recommend an investment of billions into more employment support for young people, including work placements, job subsidies and one-to-one personal advisers.

Those with more severe disabilities and unable to work would get a new benefit paid at a higher rate.

Milburn told the Times: "Candidly, it could mean that some people will get less financial support at the beginning of their benefit claim than under the current system.

"But actually, for young people, there's a different debate that we've got to resolve, which is whether the priority is their longer-term life chances or just their immediate shorter-term finances.

"I think what the current system does [is] it prioritises the latter over the former. I believe that's the wrong choice and it needs to be the other way around."

Speaking later on Thursday, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said young people would be given support "when they need it as teenagers rather than leaving them on benefits in their 20s".

He added: "The principle that we will be working on is that we will guarantee support for young people and that is the whole basis on which we will proceed."

Just under one million young people in the UK are Neets , data from the Office for National Statistics (ONS) from April to June suggests. This was a rise of 3% on the same period last year.

Milburn's recommendations are likely to be backed by Prime Minister Andy Burnham but could prove controversial among Labour MPs, who opposed welfare changes last year under his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer.

Dame Meg Hillier, who helped spearhead a backbench rebellion against Starmer's reforms, suggested she and her colleagues were broadly supportive this time around.

"What happened last year was a cut was being proposed and none of us could explain to people what would happen to them," the Labour MP told the BBC.

"Milburn has done some very good work on this so I'm giving him a fair wind," she added.

But Bell Ribeiro-Addy, one of the Labour backbenchers who revolted last year, said she was "not sure" she could vote to cut the benefit entitlement of existing claimants.

Tom Ashforth, a 19-year-old student at Sheffield Hallam University, receives both components of Pip at the higher rate.

He said the financial support helps him manage additional expenses linked to his visual impairment, including prescriptions, mobility aids and accessible learning resources.

"If I were to lose it, I would struggle to afford essential things," he said.

Student Tom said he relies on the money he gets from Pip to support him through his time at university

He said he believes decisions over disability benefits should be made on a case-by-case basis, rather than according to age.

"You cannot assume that everyone under the age of 25 is in the same position," he said.

In his Times interview, Milburn acknowledged that changing the rules for existing claimants would be "difficult politically" but stressed it was necessary.

James Taylor, from disability equality charity Scope, said Pip was a "lifeline" and restricting access to it "won't make young disabled people's extra costs disappear".

Harriet Edwards, from the charity Sense, said changes were "long overdue", but that without additional details, families were "deeply anxious".

A government spokesperson said: "We will always ensure there is a safety net for the most vulnerable and those who are unable to work."

The reforms would represent a radical overhaul of Britain's welfare system, at a time when there is heavy political pressure for the UK to find the money to spend more on defence.

Both the Conservatives and Reform UK have argued for significant cuts to welfare, including to fund a boost to defence.

Responding on Thursday, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said the government should not be spending "lots of time" on employment schemes, which she said would ultimately fail.

If Milburn's recommendations were approved, it could take almost a decade for the British state to see monetary savings.

The new system "will need significant investment" and would involve "rebuilding the system from scratch", Milburn said.

His new proposed system would involve an element of carrot and stick, wherein young people could lose some of their benefits if they did not engage with the extra work support options.

In an interview recorded on Tuesday, Skills Minister Jacqui Smith told the BBC that young people had a "responsibility" to take up employment support.

"It is a contract. People need the chance, and they need to take that chance," she added.

A separate review - co-chaired by disabilities minister Sir Stephen Timms - examining disability benefits is also expected to be published this month.

ANTALYA, Türkiye – Rwanda has called for greater investment in green industries, arguing that climate action can also drive economic growth, attract investors and create jobs.

Speaking at COP31 on Wednesday evening, Prime Minister Dr Justin Nsengiyumva said green industrialisation offers Rwanda an opportunity to address climate change while accelerating its economic transformation.

He pointed to a national programme that saves more than 30,000 tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions annually, equivalent to taking about 6,500 cars off the road.

He also urged development partners and financial institutions to move beyond pledges and form practical partnerships that share investment risks.

The Prime Minister spoke at a high-level dialogue titled “Seizing the Green Industrial Opportunity: Investment, Jobs and Growth for Every Economy”.

He delivered the remarks on behalf of President Paul Kagame.

Prime Minister Dr Justin Nsengiyumva is leading Rwanda’s delegation to COP31 including Environment Ministe Bernadette Arakwiye (left), Amb Lt Gen Rtd Charles KAYONGA – Rwanda’s envoy in Türkiye, and Teddy Mugabo, Rwanda Green Fund CEO

Nsengiyumva said green industrialisation serves two important purposes for Rwanda. It helps address the climate crisis while opening opportunities for economic growth, investment and decent jobs.

He said Rwanda’s ambitions are guided by the Green Growth and Climate Resilience Strategy, Vision 2050 and its third Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC 3.0).

Together, these frameworks set out the country’s plans to build a low-carbon economy that can also withstand the effects of climate change.

Rwanda sees opportunities in renewable energy, clean cooking, electric mobility, sustainable agriculture, the circular economy and sustainable cooling, the Prime Minister said.

Many of these sectors are also among the priorities of COP31, linking Rwanda’s development plans to the wider global effort to accelerate the green transition.

The Prime Minister cited Rwanda’s Resource Efficient and Cleaner Production Programme as an example of how green industrialisation can deliver financial returns while reducing emissions.

The programme has helped industries and small and medium-sized enterprises save more than 41 million megajoules of energy and cut annual carbon dioxide emissions by over 30,000 tonnes.

That reduction is equivalent to the annual emissions of approximately 6,500 passenger cars, using the US Environmental Protection Agency’s estimate of 4.6 tonnes of carbon dioxide per car each year.

Rwanda’s estimated fleet of 120,000 cars means the emissions reduction is comparable to taking about 5% of the country’s vehicles off the road. This is an illustration based on the emissions comparison, not a claim made by the Prime Minister.

The programme has also generated USD 6.5 million (Rwf 10 billion) in net savings from an investment of USD 5 million.

The figures show how cleaner production can help businesses reduce operating costs while lowering their environmental impact.

The Prime Minister also identified cooling as an important area for investment, as demand for cooling services continues to grow worldwide.

He pointed to the Kigali Amendment to the Montreal Protocol as an example of how climate action can support industrial development.

Full implementation of the amendment could prevent up to half a degree Celsius of global warming by 2100, while creating jobs in manufacturing, equipment servicing and cold-chain services.

He called for its full ratification and swift implementation.

Rwanda has already established a foundation for investment in the sector through its National Cooling Strategy, minimum energy-performance standards and financing mechanisms, he added.

The Prime Minister said expanding green industries would require governments, development partners and financial institutions to share investment risks.

He identified blended finance, concessional loans, guarantees and carbon finance as important tools for making green industrial projects financially viable and attractive to investors.

He urged development partners and financial institutions to move “beyond commitments to practical partnerships” that produce measurable economic, social and environmental benefits.

Lydia Dibben wants more small farms around Wales growing produce

Droughts and wildfires in the summer were a wake-up call, and winter flooding could leave Wales' food supply vulnerable, an expert has warned.

The country currently imports the vast majority of its fruit and vegetables, with only 6% of those served in its schools grown in Wales.

It is dependent on produce from parts of the world prone to droughts and fires, according to co-founder of an organisation aiming to address this.

Duncan Fisher is behind Our Food Trust , external , which wants to build 100 farms, producing fruit and vegetables in Wales for local markets.

Despite 90% of the country being used for agriculture , external , only about 0.1% is currently being used for horticulture , external .

Growers at Fisher's Wern Farm, near Newtown, Powys, said this must change if the country is to survive climate change, wars and other global disruptions to the supply chain.

"We are hugely dependent and these vegetables are coming from really vulnerable parts of the world like south Europe and north Africa - the areas most prone to drought, fires and overheating," said Fisher.

Food security has become a hot topic , with Defence Secretary Wes Streeting saying in October people should have water, tinned goods, baby food, torches and mobile phone charging packs ready in case of emergency.

Fisher referenced this appeal, adding the UK "has an incredibly centralised food system with 95% of the food we eat bought from nine supermarkets".

He said: "There's no storage, it's a just-in-time system so the food is stored in lorries moving across motorways.

"That is a security hazard because it's very vulnerable to cyber-attacks.

"If the system goes wrong, there's no resilience in it. The food just runs out straight away."

Duncan Fisher said he has hope that Wales will be able to increase its fruit and veg growing

Fisher and Sue Holbrook launched Our Food Trust about 10 years ago with the aim of growing more produce locally for local markets.

They found one of the main barriers was stable housing for farmers.

As Fisher explained: "If there's a high wind during the night, they need to get out there and protect things.

"If a sheep gets in, they have to get the sheep out before the entire thing is destroyed in an hour. So they have to live there."

But he said planning regulations have made it really difficult to build homes on farmland.

However, by working with Powys council and Bannau Brycheiniog National Park Authority, they have been able to build three temporary homes for farmers on 36 acres of council-owned land.

Lydia Dibben, one of the growers, said even though it was a difficult year they were able to grow a lot of food

One of the growers at Wern Farm is Lydia Dibben, 28, and she agreed access to land is one of the biggest barriers to new farmers.

She said if her home was not provided she would have to get another job to be able to afford rent, and then would end up without enough time to farm.

"I'm only growing on about just over an acre this year, and we're now doing 50 veg boxes a week," she said.

"We've been doing four farmers' markets a month up until the beginning of October. We're also supplying into regional and national wholesale as well.

"I don't know how many people we're feeding, but it's got to be hundreds of people on just a couple of acres."

She believes there are lots of people who want to do similar work, and they should be given access to land and affordable housing to do so.

Lydia Dibben said she got into growing vegetables in lockdown and decided this was what she wanted to do as a job

Dibben said she believed people in the UK thought it would be able to "avoid many of the real challenges of climate breakdown" and "just be able to grow grapes and peaches" but the reality is very different.

"We're going to have to really think a lot harder about how we're producing food, even in this country," she said.

This includes looking at which vegetables work best in hotter climates.

Dibben described the past summer as the hardest she had experienced in five years of growing.

"The hours I was keeping were just insane," she said.

"I was getting out to the field at 05:00, and then working until it got just too hot to be outside, which was like 11:00 some days, maybe even earlier."

She said working in polytunnels was impossible by 09:00 due to the heat.

When it became too hot to work, she had to go indoors and "just survive until it was cool enough to go back outside at probably 17:00".

She then worked until midnight to try and get everything watered.

Dibben said she did not usually have to worry too much about not having enough water, but this year was completely different.

"Even the things that you felt like you were giving as much water as you could were still not growing as much as they should be," she added.

"We've not had the water bill yet for this summer, but I dread to think.

"We've just not had the crops to make it worth it."

Lydia Dibben said every day is different on the farm

She does not believe it will necessarily be as bad every year, but Dibben accepts there will be more hot summers and unpredictable weather such as flooding.

Dibben thinks there will always be a need for bigger scale farms producing wheat, barley, beef or sheep.

"But I think if there was a farm like ours every 10 miles throughout Wales, that would be a pretty great future in my eyes," she added.

The Welsh government said "significant progress" had been made on its plans to create a national food strategy to "target a more resilient, integrated and sustainable food system".

"There will also be a focus on how to grow more fruit and vegetables in Wales, and we have already begun mapping the current position of the sector with key stakeholders," said a spokesperson.

The UK government's Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) said: "We recognise the hurdles that our vital fruit and vegetable growers face, which is why we are slashing planning red tape and investing £200m to help farmers trial crop boosting technology.

"The prime minister has made clear that food security is national security, and we're working across the farming sector to make supply chains more resilient."

The clocks have gone back, it's getting darker and colder, which could mean you may find the winter months particularly hard.

Rachel Dineen-Mabe is one of more than a million people with Seasonal Affective Disorder (Sad) , external in the UK, and says it "takes depression and heightens it to a whole new level".

But a new scheme allowing people to borrow Sad lamps from libraries has been launched across Wales to help combat the darker days.

Sad happens when shorter days affect your mood, energy levels and overall wellbeing.

Rachel, 38, the branch librarian at Skewen Library, said darker days make it hard to do anything.

"I struggle just getting out of bed sometimes, I just want to hibernate," she said.

"I don't want to do anything but sleep and it is a real struggle to carry on doing normal everyday things from just dressing, not necessarily because you don't want to but you physically feel unable to."

With libraries having long moved on from just offering book loans, Rachel said schemes such as this are "vital"

Rachel, whose library is in one of the 11 council areas taking part in the free lamps scheme, said she notices the effects from about October.

She said: "It's a shame because for me, it's a lovely time of year. I love it, but it has this low mood hanging over it that just leaves it feeling a bit sad.

"I make a real effort to get out as much as I can, obviously my job is very people-focused so I'm always speaking with people which is lovely because this is a lovely community.

"I'm a big reader so that helps and I have bright lights at home like twinkly lights or ambient light all year round, to just try and boost the mood."

The lamps mimic sunlight to help boost mood, energy and sleep cycles

"I've used the Sad lamps before and it feels like just a little bit of sunshine in a day where maybe you've seen nothing, it really does boost your mood."

Rachel said that getting outside was the best advice she could give to someone experiencing Sad symptoms.

She said: "I know it's hard but get outside if you can, speak to people. Like I've said, talking about mental health is such an important thing at the moment and this is part of it.

"There are so many people who have Sad and may not even know it, and it's good to acknowledge it."

Lorna herself uses a Sad lamp to help the days "feel brighter"

Lorna Beatrice Lombardini, 26, from Cardiff Bay, said it was tough being a student during the winter months.

"You're inside a lot of the time, working deadlines, exams, and then trying to still have a social life at the same time plus work," she said.

"I absolutely love the 'say yes' idea, which is even if you get invited to plans, you're thinking it's too cold, it's too dark, I want to stay inside. Just say yes.

"Even if you go and it doesn't turn out how you want it to go, you can go home and still appreciate home that little bit more but it's always the experiences that you're not expecting that turn out to be the best."

She said she already uses lamps to help her with mood, and does feel an improvement.

"I know that this is a very universal experience but whatever I can do to try and lift the mood a little bit, feel a little bit lighter, I do try and do my best," she said.

Eleven Welsh councils are taking part in the scheme, developed by researchers from the universities of Glasgow and Edinburgh with funding from the Economic and Social Research Council.

It forms part of a wider expansion across the UK, following two years of trials in Scotland.

The lamps on loan retail at £99, but there are cheaper ones on the market.

Hester Parr, from the University of Glasgow, said the boxes available to borrow had been put together based on research of those with lived experience of Sad and contain a booklet, an online course and a lamp.

"The whole intention of the box is to help people who feel low mood in winter, or feel that they have Seasonal Affective Disorder, make some kind of positive change," she said.

"This is outside the GP system, it's free to use from your local library, so there's no stigma attached to getting this lovely resource that helps us live well in winter."

Emily Van de Venter, from Public Health Wales, said: "People that have been part of the trials have reported benefits and wanted to continue accessing the Sad lamps, evidence has been growing around the benefits that these lamps can bring."

She advised using them for about 20 minutes in the morning, and then gain as much daylight exposure during the day as possible.

The boxes are available across Cardiff, Swansea, Wrexham, Neath Port Talbot, Blaenau Gwent, Merthyr Tydfil, Powys, Conwy, Newport, Vale of Glamorgan and Caerphilly.

Dr Doris Uwicyeza Picard, Chief Executive Officer of the Rwanda Governance Board, speaking at event last year

KIGALI – The Rwanda Governance Board (RGB) has identified negative narratives about Rwanda’s governance as one of the threats facing the country, according to its new 2026–2029 Strategic Plan.

The plan does not propose a specific programme to fight such narratives. Instead, RGB says it will focus on producing research, publishing governance reports, engaging citizens and improving public services.

The four-year plan has a budget of Rwf7.3 billion. It lists negative narratives in its SWOT analysis of the country’s governance agenda.

One of RGB’s main approaches will be to produce more research on governance and citizens’ experiences with public services. It plans to conduct at least 25 studies and publish 30 policy briefs by 2029.

The board also wants to make more governance reports available to the public, increasing their accessibility from 35% to 100% by 2029.

Another part of the plan involves taking Rwanda’s Home-Grown Solutions to international audiences. Working with the Rwanda Cooperation Initiative, RGB plans to document at least 20 such solutions and share them through international exchanges and cooperation programmes.

The board also plans to work with government institutions, civil society groups, businesses, religious organisations and development partners to promote public engagement and share information about Rwanda’s governance experience. It targets at least 20 formal partnerships by 2029.

However, the plan places considerable emphasis on improving governance itself. RGB wants compliance with service delivery standards to rise from 45% to at least 90%, while at least 85% of public complaints should be resolved within set timelines.

NHS funding is one of the biggest challenges facing Plaid Cymru ministers

Senior Welsh NHS bosses are calling on the Welsh government to provide multi-year funding settlements for health rather than relying on annual budgets.

Next week, ministers will unveil draft spending plans for all public services for the 2027-28 financial year.

The NHS accounts for almost half of the Welsh government's £27.5bn annual budget, but health leaders say one-year funding settlements can constrain long-term planning and transformation.

A Welsh government spokesperson said it was "working to improve services now while making the longer-term changes needed".

The call comes from the Welsh NHS Alliance , external , formerly the Welsh NHS Confederation, ahead of evidence sessions at the Senedd's health committee on Thursday examining spending plans for 2027-28.

Tuesday's draft budget will need support from at least one opposition party to secure Senedd approval.

Talks between the Welsh government and opposition parties were ongoing.

Last week, the minority Welsh government relied on Labour support to pass adjustments to its spending plans for the next five months, including an extra £100m to help cut NHS waiting times.

In written evidence, the alliance warned that annual budgeting can make it harder to deliver long-term changes to the health service.

"There is a risk that annual planning cycles can constrain longer-term transformation, where benefits often require multi-year investment before being realised," it said.

The organisation argued ministers should prioritise spending that helps "shift Wales from a system focused on treating illness to one that creates health and wellbeing".

It added: "This requires multi-year funding certainty and transparent criteria for investment and disinvestment."

The alliance also cautioned against making cuts to broad service areas in isolation.

"The health and care system is highly interconnected, and reducing expenditure in one area can simply displace costs elsewhere, often into more expensive urgent and emergency care," it said.

It argued spending decisions should instead be based on "value, outcomes and whole-system impact".

The alliance added: "The NHS cannot sustainably meet future demand if resources remain concentrated predominantly at the point of crisis."

It called for more investment in primary and community care, rehabilitation, public health services and support for people with long-term conditions.

Council leaders responsible for social services, who will also give evidence to the committee, warned the sector was under "considerable pressure".

In written evidence, they said councils remained broadly confident of meeting their legal duties, but warned of growing concerns about the long-term sustainability of services if current trends continue.

Like NHS leaders, they also called for multi-year funding settlements.

A Welsh government spokesperson said: "We are working to improve services now while making the longer-term changes needed.

"That means a stronger focus on prevention, reducing health inequalities and supporting independent living, with services designed around outcomes rather than responding to demand."

The marketplace is sometimes called the 'eBay' of Lego

Lego has taken its online marketplace BrickLink offline after detecting what it described as unusual activity on the platform.

BrickLink is used by Lego collectors worldwide to buy and sell second-hand sets, source new bricks and purchase limited edition releases.

It was originally set up by a fan but acquired by Lego in 2019. The firm wrote on its homepage that before restoring BrickLink, it wanted to "fully understand" what had happened.

"That means containing the issue, investigating how it happened and checking for related issues," Lego said. It did not provide any further detail about whether the site had been breached or hacked, nor whether any customer data had been affected.

Lego published the update after being contacted by the BBC.

BrickLink has been offline for the last three days, with a previous message saying it was down for maintenance.

Cyber-professional Melanie Hoskin has been collecting Lego for 45 years and is a regular user of BrickLink.

She told the BBC she had received multiple links for payment for a limited edition release she had pre-ordered on the platform after she had already paid for it.

She said Lego did not believe that the payment had been taken and at one point said it would ban her from BrickLink.

Melanie Hoskin has been collecting Lego for 45 years

The problem has now been resolved and Lego said it was not aware of wider payment issues.

It is unclear whether the payment glitch had any connection to the issue that led to the website going offline.

Hoskin said she felt like she had been accused of theft.

"Lego is my stress relief," she said. "Lego is what I grew up with as a kid, it's what bonded me with my sisters.

"I've got a Lego room and I've not even been able to walk into it this past couple of weeks because it just angers me."

Earlier today, a message on BrickLink said the platform would be back online by Wednesday evening, but that message has now been deleted and there is no longer a time frame given for its return.

Simbarashe Kundizeza, who lives in Harare, says he was inspired by a poem about fish tanks to write a story about his family struggles

The Caine Prize for African Writing has said that after an internal review it has found no evidence that Zimbabwean writer Simbarashe Kundizeza had used generative AI to write his winning short story and confirmed him as the winner of this year's £10,000 ($13,000) award.

Ellah Wakatama, chair of the Caine Prize's board of trustees, said the matter had been investigated following an article in US magazine The Atlantic with the headline, Yet Another Literary Prizewinner Seems to Be AI.

"From our detailed investigation, we feel the evidence is clear: The Blue Fighter was human written," she said in a video posted on X.

The accusation had caused a social media uproar and Kundizeza had denied the allegation.

The Atlantic article by journalist Vauhini Vara alleged that AI-detection software Pangram had shown his work about a boy whose family falls on hard times was entirely AI generated.

Her allegations followed rows over other literary prizes this year, in particular the Commonwealth Short Story Prize, which was won by Trinidadian writer Jamir Nazir despite allegations that he had used AI, and the withdrawal of Canadian-Haitian author Thélyson Orélien from France's top literary award, the Goncourt, over allegations he used AI for his first novel, which he denies .

Following the publication of her article last month, Vara had told BBC's Front Row programme that every other previous Caine Prize winning story she had put through Pangram "came out as 100% human".

The backlash on social media included comments from African writers with suggestions that such accusations are primarily being made against non-white writers.

Zimbabwean author denies using AI to write award-winning story

Wakatama said the Caine Prize organisation had considered Vara's allegations "carefully and fairly".

"We chose to take a human-centred approach to the investigation. Our review included interviews with the author, the 2026 judging panel, and the Shallow Tales Review, where the story was first published," she said.

"It also included independent and expert-led metadata analysis of drafts written by the author."

In a statement, the Caine Prize explained further that the analysis had been conducted by an independent cyber security and digital forensic investigator , external .

The day after winning the prestigious Caine Prize award earlier in October, Kundizeza had told the BBC he was inspired after hearing a poem read by South African Vangile Gantsho at an event in Ghana last year about her father's obsession with building fish tanks.

He said he had weaved that with fictionalised details from his own life around 2002 when Zimbabwe's economic troubles began.

If production is approved, oil and gas will be pumped up through a large ship 80 miles north west of Shetland

Some Labour MPs have called on the government to reject the Rosebank oil field, saying it is "incompatible" with the UK's climate commitments.

There is a growing expectation among senior Labour figures that drilling in the oil field off the north-west coast of Shetland will be given the go-ahead.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Wednesday that a decision would be "taken in due course" while Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh stressed that affordability of energy bills was her "overriding objective".

But in a sign of the division within the party, more than a dozen Labour MPs expressed concerns in Parliament about approving it. Others expressed support, pointing to economic benefits.

Supportive Labour MPs said some other parts of the world emitted far more greenhouse gases than the UK and warned of relying on imports. Reports have suggested that Chancellor John Healey is in favour of approval.

Separately, it is understood some Labour backbenchers have organised a letter opposing Rosebank - intended for Burnham, but not yet sent - which more than 60 out of about 400 Labour MPs have indicated they support.

One signatory told the BBC that approving Rosebank "would not create new jobs, would bring minimal money into the Treasury and be bad for the climate".

"The government's central aim is to tackle the cost of living crisis, and drilling for more oil at Rosebank isn't the answer," the MP said.

Wednesday's Westminster Hall - a type of parliamentary debate where backbench MPs raise topical issues but do not vote - was organised by Green MP Carla Denyer.

Labour MP for Sheffield Central Abtisam Mohamed told the debate: "Rosebank fails on every test.

"It will not benefit taxpayers who will shoulder the vast majority of the development costs, it will not strengthen our energy security because most of the oil will be sold on international markets, and it will not reduce energy bills for our constituents, who will remain exposed to volatile fossil fuel prices."

Richard Burgon, a former frontbencher on the left of the party, said: "Rosebank is not compatible with our climate targets - it's dangerous to pretend otherwise."

The UK is committed to reaching net zero by 2050 and wants to limit global warming to no more than 1.5C above the pre-industrial period.

The UK government has always insisted that Rosebank is a quasi-judicial decision, formally resting with Fahnbulleh . She green-lit production in the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea last month, but Rosebank hangs in the balance.

Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh will formally announce the Rosebank decision, expected in the coming weeks

Labour's manifesto upon entering power in 2024 pledged not to "issue new licences to explore new fields".

Licences for both Jackdaw and Rosebank were granted by the then Conservative UK government in 2022 and 2023 respectively.

But the Court of Session in Edinburgh ruled last year that the government had made the approvals unlawfully, leaving the current Labour government to make a fresh decision on whether to give the go-ahead.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch sought to tease at Labour divisions on the issue during Prime Minister's Questions on Wednesday.

During the debate, Labour MP Anna Gelderd said: "We live in an unprecedented era where our energy security is more vital than ever, in which jobs and wealth must be protected and economic opportunities seized - on both of these points, Rosebank fails."

Labour MP Julia Buckley said she had received opposition to Rosebank from her constituents in "regularly flooded Shrewsbury" and said fossil fuels "belong in the past, not the future".

She urged Fahnbulleh to "reject the oil licence in favour of renewables", adding: "Please don't add further to our climate emergency."

Other Labour MPs expressed their support, including recently departed veterans minister Al Carns, who warned that Britain would continue to need fossil fuels for decades and importing more would be a mistake.

"Refusing to produce it here does nothing on its own to eliminate that demand - it simply increases our reliance on imports which can carry their own environmental cost," he added.

Those representing communities with ties to the oil and gas industry, including Jonathan Brash, the Labour MP for Hartlepool, stressed the benefits of approving Rosebank for British jobs.

Speaking to BBC Radio 5 Live, Labour MP Bill Esterson, chair of Energy Security and Net Zero Committee, said "the economics of it (Rosebank) are that you should carry on with it" and "there's an element of energy security" by approving it.

Energy minister Michael Shanks told the debate the government would take a "pragmatic approach" to a clean energy transition, stressing it was "not a turn off the taps government, but nor can we justifiably be a drill every last drop government either".

"This government will not make decisions for this country which are not compatible with our climate obligations," he added.

Watch: Moment historic ship sinks off the coast of Florida

A ship that was once the fastest in the world and is longer than the Titanic has intentionally been sunk off the coast of Florida, turning into the world's largest artificial ocean reef.

The SS United States spent nearly 30 years docked in Philadelphia before it was moved to Florida, where it will become a home for sealife and an underwater attraction for marine enthusiasts.

Activists unsuccessfully fought for the historic liner - which crossed the Atlantic Ocean hundreds of times - to be preserved as a museum.

Instead, after being purchased by a Florida county, it was added to the dozens of artificial reefs off the coast, with a land-based museum detailing the ship's history also planned.

Before its retirement, the SS United States was known for carrying royalty and celebrities between the US and Europe, beginning in 1952 and ending in 1969.

A young Bill Clinton, before he was president, used the ship to cross the Atlantic. Former presidents Harry Truman, Dwight Eisenhower and John Kennedy also travelled on the vessel.

The ship was moved from Philadelphia to Alabama last year for cleaning and remediation work.

On Monday, it took its final journey from Alabama to the coast of Destin, Florida, where it was sunk on Wednesday in a precision operation without explosives.

This archival video shows the SS United States in 2025 as it starts its move to Florida on its way to become the world's largest artificial reef.

Stars including Marlon Brando, Coco Chanel, Duke Ellington, Salvador Dali, Walt Disney, Judy Garland and Cary Grant also boarded the ship during its sailing lifetime.

Before its purchase by the municipal Florida government, a number of proposals that would have seen the ship live a second life as a museum or a floating hotel failed.

Instead, it sat at various docks with various owners as legal battles played out.

The SS United States Conservancy group repeatedly attempted to keep the ship above water, but was unsuccessful.

Conservancy President Susan Gibbs - whose grandfather helped design the liner - said she was glad that the story of the SS United States would live on.

"[The ship] has always been this unabashedly American symbol that brings so many people together," Gibbs told CBS News, the BBC's US partner.

Watch: Author says she was 'warned' about David Walliams' behaviour

Author Chloe Combi has said she had heard rumours that there were "real concerns" about David Walliams's behaviour within the publishing industry more than a decade ago.

Combi told BBC News she had heard there were allegations about his "behaviour around young female staff" and says she was told in 2015 to warn schools that he was "not an appropriate booking".

An investigation by the Guardian and ITV News alleged that Walliams has been accused by several women of sexual misconduct, inappropriate behaviour and abusing his position, which he denies.

HarperCollins, which published Walliams's best-selling children's books, dropped Walliams last year after an investigation into his behaviour.

In response to the Guardian and ITV report, a spokesperson for HarperCollins said the company had decided not to publish any new titles by Walliams and that it took "employee wellbeing extremely seriously".

Walliams told ITV News and the Guardian that he was "not a sexual predator" and had not "broken the law".

Combi said she was getting invited to events such as book launches around the time one of her own books was being published, and was also running a scheme to bring "high-profile and inspiring writers and speakers" to talk in schools.

At an event in 2015, Combi said she got speaking to someone "quite senior" in publishing, who warned her about Walliams.

"We were talking about [the scheme] and possible writers who might be good for the project to work well with teenagers," Combi said.

"She gave me some great recommendations and said to me: 'Whatever you do, don't invite David Walliams, and FYI if you are speaking to head teachers or teachers, please inform them that he's not a good booking, not an appropriate booking for a school'."

Combi continued: "I obviously asked why, and to be honest I had already heard quite a lot of rumours because those worlds are quite small and contained.

"One of the things she said was that there had been real concerns about his behaviour around young female staff."

If you are affected by any of the issues in this story, help and support is available at BBC Action Line.

Asked whether concerns about his behaviour was an open secret, Combi replied: "Yes definitely... and I'd heard it from people who worked in publishing, fellow writers, people kind of in celebrity and TV circles."

Combi said she never met Walliams herself, and said her information had come from "a number of people I was speaking to".

HarperCollins in September announced it would no longer be publishing his back catalogue.

The allegations against Walliams include:

One woman alleges she met Walliams at a fan event when she was 15. She says he groomed her and they had sex when she was 17

Another woman alleges she met Walliams for a coffee when she was 15, before going back to his house where he allegedly tried to lift up her shirt and commit an act that she now describes as a sexual assault

A woman who worked as a model in her teens accused Walliams of grooming her. A different woman who also worked as a model said Walliams tried to kiss her while showing her around his home

The investigation claimed Walliams had a sexual relationship with at least one junior employee at publisher HarperCollins, and pursued another

Other women allege inappropriate behaviour at ITV's Britain's Got Talent, such as inviting girls and young women to his dressing room

In his statement to ITV News and the Guardian, Walliams said: "Looking back, I realise that at times I behaved thoughtlessly towards other people I had casual sexual relationships with.

"I realise I did not always take people's feelings properly into account. That is something I regret. And whilst a power imbalance is inevitable when one party is famous, abusing that power is something else entirely and it is something that I never did."

He added: "I am not a sexual predator. I have not broken the law, but I am devastated that some of the women I met 10 to 20 years ago have now expressed hurt or anger towards me."

What we know about the allegations against David Walliams

Earlier on Wednesday, media minister Ian Murray said there is a "cultural problem" in the industry that needs to be "stamped out".

Giving evidence to the Digital, Culture, Media and Sport Committee, Murray said he was "deeply saddened and also angry" to see the prevalence of abuse by men in the media industry.

Meanwhile, Minister for Women and Equalities Bridget Phillipson paid tribute to the "bravery" of victims who have shared their experiences in recent days.

Speaking in the Commons, she said: "Women and girls should never have to shrink our lives or ambitions because of outdated, misogynistic attitudes, and the appalling testimonies we have heard in recent days underline how much further we have to go."

Phillipson later said the government would "go further" on restricting the use of non-disclosure agreements, telling Sky News: "We cannot have a system where rich and powerful individuals, rich and powerful men, are able to silence women, buy their silence and stop things coming to light."

She said that she believed injunctions were being misused, and that her colleagues at the Ministry of Justice were looking at how the government can intervene to ensure this did not happen.

Comedian and podcaster Deborah Frances-White told BBC Radio 4's The World at One that young women are "definitely" still being exploited in the comedy industry.

She told the programme that perpetrators understand consent but they just enjoy the power that comes with ignoring it, adding: "The thrill is in the contravention of consent."

Asked whether she recognised the picture Russell Brand's conviction and allegations against Walliams had painted of the comedy industry, she said: "Yes, entirely."

She described an industry where she was asked to meet male producers in darkly lit rooms "walking a tightrope", having to make them feel attractive and avoid being assaulted as they influenced future employment opportunities.

She said these events are "definitely still going on" and that she is in a WhatsApp group with female comedians who share their experiences with each other.

Comedian Lucy Beaumont told Sky News that she was one of the people who spoke to the Guardian about allegations raised with her about Walliams.

Beaumont said she had been approached by a young TV worker who alleged inappropriate behaviour while working with Walliams on another show.

"This young person's job was to take young girls - he didn't think that they were children... he definitely knew that they were over 16 - he had to take them to Walliams's dressing room," she alleged.

Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme on Wednesday, Labour MP Jess Phillips said the behaviour alleged "needs to be stopped".

"What is described in the David Walliams story is an absolute modus operandi, a target group of women of a certain age, the kind of women who don't have the same amount of power as if you were doing this to a 35-year-old woman who might have a bit more about herself in the world," she said.

Iyi mibare yatangajwe na Minisitiri w’Intebe w’u Rwanda mu kiganiro cyabereye muri Antalya muri Türkiye, ku wa 11 Ugushyingo 2026, cyari gifite insanganyamatsiko igira iti “Gukoresha amahirwe y’inganda zishingiye ku bukungu butangiza ibidukikije: Ishoramari, imirimo n’iterambere ry’ubukungu”.

Yasobanuye ko gahunda y’u Rwanda yo guteza imbere umusaruro ushingiye ku gukoresha neza umutungo no kugabanya ingaruka ku bidukikije yafashije inganda n’ibigo bito n’ibiciriritse kugabanya ingufu byakoreshaga ku rugero rwa megajoules zisaga miliyoni 41, ndetse n’ibyuka bihumanya ku rugero rwa toni zirenga 30.000 za gaz carbonique (CO₂) buri mwaka.

Megajoules ni igipimo cy'ingufu. Ni ukuvuga ingano y'ingufu zishobora gukoreshwa mu gukora umurimo runaka, nko guteka, gucana, gukoresha imashini mu ruganda cyangwa gutwara imodoka.

Minisitiri w’Intebe yavuze ko ibi bigaragaza ko guteza imbere inganda zirengera ibidukikije atari igisubizo ku mihindagurikire y’ikirere gusa, ahubwo ko ari n’amahirwe yo kongera umusaruro, gukurura ishoramari no guhanga imirimo.

Yagaragaje ko u Rwanda rwifuza kwagura ishoramari muri uru rwego, cyane cyane mu mishinga y’ingufu zisubira, uburyo bwo guteka butangiza ibidukikije, ibinyabiziga bikoresha amashanyarazi, ubuhinzi burambye, kongera gukoresha ibikoresho byajugunywe ndetse n’ikoranabuhanga ryo gukonjesha ritangiza ibidukikije.

Watch: County Sheriff describes how buried baby was found

An 11-month-old baby has been rescued in South Carolina after officials say he was buried alive in a crate by his father.

Koah Sharpe had been missing since Monday when he was taken by his father, Michael Comer, 25, according to the Lexington County Sheriff's Department. Comer was arrested on a burglary charge on Monday evening but his son was not with him.

The baby was found on Tuesday "buried alive" and "clinging to life" not far from his father's house, Lexington County Sheriff Jay Koon said at a news conference. It is thought he had been there for 24 hours.

The child is now in hospital receiving care, Koon said, adding he was hopeful he would make a full recovery.

Police are still deciding what further charges to bring against the father.

The search for baby Koah began on Monday after his father took him from his mother's house.

Comer's mother was watching the child and had left her son alone with him briefly, Koon said, when he left abruptly with Koah.

Officials allege the baby's father buried him alive in a dog crate

Comer was seen travelling to multiple locations without the baby and was later arrested in Lexington County without Koah. A search party of 100 police and fire department officials were then sent to search for the child, the sheriff said.

He added that when they asked Comer where his son was, he "did not have much to say" about his whereabouts.

Koon said that rescuers searched the woods near Comer's house and saw some "freshly disturbed dirt". As they began to dig, they heard a baby crying - something the sheriff described as "the most joyful sound you ever heard".

"The race was on. Everybody was getting down there trying to get him out," Koon added.

He said the crate was wrapped in a towel that probably provided enough air for Koah to survive for as long as he did, while the cold weather kept him from getting too hot.

"The crate was, probably, I'm guessing about a two-foot [61cm] by two-foot dog crate. So, I think, once that crate hit the ground, he was probably up at least a foot from the top of that crate to the top of the ground," Koon explained.

Of the parents' relationship, the sheriff said there were "obviously some issues". Comer had previously pleaded guilty to domestic violence charges, court records show.

Comer's mother, Patricia Comer, told NBC News that Koah's mother had full custody of him but allowed her to supervise while her son watched him. She said her son had watched the baby before unsupervised without any problems.

"Honestly, I'm his mother, and I never expected this from him," Patricia Comer said.

Shrewsbury Town's new sporting director Brad Friedel's previous coaching experience is chiefly at international level

Shrewsbury Town's new sporting director Brad Friedel says the League Two club are the perfect project for the new American owners following a Europe-wide search.

Miami-based Scott Davidson's Biscayne ST LLC consortium, of which Friedel is part, completed their majority takeover on Monday, buying 87.4% of the shares, allowing long-time owner Roland Wycherley to relinquish control after 30 years.

"Scott and I met through friends in Miami and through the love of football, nothing more or less," former USA goalkeeper Friedel told BBC Radio Shropshire in an exclusive interview.

"As we got to know each other, our thoughts on business and football aligned. We got to the point where we said let's try to find a club which fits a whole bunch of criteria."

Brad Friedel on Shrewsbury Town takeover

Friedel group completes Shrewsbury Town takeover

"We looked in Turkey, Poland, Portugal and Holland but, at the clubs we were looking, something didn't align for one reason or another. A lot of it came down to 'Did we think our group can help the football club?' We want to bring the town firmly behind the club."

Wycherley first announced his plans to find a successor five years ago and Friedel says, with Davidson already being a majority shareholder of Edinburgh-based The Spartans in Scottish League Two, they wanted a club they could take forward.

"The one-town club really appealed. We want to integrate the club even more into the town than it is now. When you look at the investment going into the EFL, the foreign investment, there's a reason for it. There's no better place for football than the United Kingdom.

"Once we decided our group would be best suited to the UK market, Shrewsbury hit all the boxes. But also what we feel we can deliver towards the club and the town."

Shrewsbury takeover in 'final stages' - Wycherley

As a player, Friedel spent the majority of his club career in the Premier League with Liverpool, Blackburn Rovers, Aston Villa and Tottenham Hotspur, but the 55-year-old is unfazed about taking his first sporting director role in England's fourth tier.

"I don't look at football anymore as I would only take a job in the Premier League or the Champions League," he said. "One of my most enjoyable jobs post-playing career was being head coach of the US men's under-19 national team and most of those players weren't even professional.

"I look at football opportunities with different projects. The upside, if you get it right in English football, is there is such a buzz for me out of it, so I don't look at this as an EFL League Two club, I look at is as another incredible project with incredible people."

Shrewsbury finished 10 points clear of relegation in League Two last season, having appointed former player Gavin Cowan as head coach in January to help steer them clear of a drop into the National League - and Friedel intends to work closely with him.

"I'm moving over here," he added. "I'll be there day-to-day so this is not a situation where you'll see me every now and then at the club. I'm not here for the short term.

"It'll be a collaboration. The way we see football being successful is you have to have roles and structure but you can't have dictators. Gavin and I will be around each other every day. I'll be at training every day.

"It's a group effort. If we're successful it will have nothing to do with just what I do or Scott does or Gavin does. It's everybody on and off the field who has to pull their weight for us to be successful."

One area the new owners intend to concentrate on is recruitment - and Friedel is already at work identifying potential new signings.

"I'm very much data driven but I'd never sign a player just on data as there are so many different elements to signing a player," he said.

"What data does is speed up the process. We have our own customised platform and we'll be bringing in other individuals to help with the recruitment process. We'll collaborate with Gavin and extend a much wider net around the globe.

"We will reach out to many parts of the world that have not been previously by Shrewsbury Town. We're excited about bringing this recruitment department in. It's something that's already in place. They're here and we're already working."

This is a second season in League Two for Shrewsbury, whose 10-season stay in League One ended in 2025.

They last played in the second tier in 1989 but Friedel is not ruling out the club returning to that level at some point in the future.

"Everything is possible," he said. "You've got to dream but let's take one thing at a time. We want to come in and take this step-by-step.

"We want to be possible promotion contenders, whether it's this season or next. That's our aim. If we're fortunate enough to get up into League One we'll try to do it again and, if we get up into the Championship, that's another formidable task.

"We want to baby-step this. First stability, structure and make sure we're providing the resources needed for the first-team staff, for the players to be successful and for the academy to be successful and then see where we go."

MN202611_ztwb93o8np.t:
Guidance already exists to restrict heading in training in England and Scotland

An MP is calling for legal safeguards to limit repetitive heading in football training, amid growing concerns about the risk of brain injury.

Grahame Morris, the Labour MP for Easington, submitted a parliamentary motion on Tuesday urging the government to take action to reduce the number of times a player can head the ball in training.

Researchers have found footballers are three and a half times more likely to die from a neurodegenerative disease than the general population.

The Early Day Motion (EDM) describes the need to protect players' brain health as a "significant public health and player welfare issue".

"The aim of this EDM is to raise awareness of the growing body of evidence linking repeated head impacts, particularly from heading a football, to an increased risk of neurodegenerative disease," Morris told BBC Sport.

The motion encourages the government "to take a more active role in prevention, education and player protection" Morris added.

Morris's motion supports a national petition submitted in September by the charity Head Safe Football, and calls on the government to take a number of actions:

Impose legal limits on repetitive heading in football training

Establish a cross-departmental task-force involving medical experts, players representatives, campaign groups and football authorities to develop "enforceable heading safeguards"

Recognise chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) as a public health concern

Create a national action plan to protect players' brain health

Improve education and awareness of the risks associated with heading, including in schools and through the PE national curriculum

EDMs are seen as a means for MPs to express their opinion on a subject and to canvass support for their views. No matter how many MPs sign up to an EDM there is no guarantee that it will be debated in Parliament.

Football does already have restrictions around heading.

The Football Association has phased out deliberate heading in grassroots football matches for children aged 11 and under.

It has also issued guidance recommending limits on heading during training of no more than 10 headers per week at amateur level.

In the professional game in England, clubs have been advised to limit players to 10 "high force" headers a week in training.

Scotland has gone further, banning heading in training on the day before and after matches in the professional game.

However, campaigners such as Dr Judith Gates, founder of Head Safe Football, believe that voluntary guidance is not enough.

"What we are finding is that coaches and parents don't know of the guidance, or the ban. Or they do not know why it exists," she told BBC Sport.

"There needs to be greater clarity and greater specific restrictions in order to protect players of today and tomorrow."

Dr Gates, whose husband the former Middlesbrough player Bill died with CTE, a degenerative brain disease associated with repeated head impacts, accepts that enforcing a legal limit would be challenging.

The calls for greater protection came as Prime Minister Andy Burnham called, in an interview with the Telegraph, , external on English football to formally recognise the game's dementia crisis and establish an "industrial injuries" compensation scheme for former players.

In a statement to BBC Sport, he said: "I've spoken to families affected by dementia and brain injury and heard what they have been through.

"Their determination to get this issue taken seriously has been extraordinary, and they should never have had to fight so hard to be heard."

Burnham's intervention follows inquests into the deaths of former England World Cup winner Nobby Stiles and Scotland defender Gordon McQueen, which found repetitive heading had contributed to their deaths.

The Professional Footballer's association (PFA) and the Premier League set up a brain health fund which has provided about £1m annually since 2023. However, campaigners say this is not enough to meet the costs of care.

The Football Association has not financially contributed to the fund, but said it continued to invest in research and had introduced guidance across professional and grassroots football.

"While the link between heading in football and long-term brain health remains the subject of ongoing scientific and medical research, we have consistently been at the forefront of efforts to help improve the safety of our game," an FA spokesperson said.

MN202611_1mbouhjgrw5.t:
Dara O'Shea stepped in as Republic of Ireland captain for the last international window in place of the injured Nathan Collins

Republic of Ireland defender Dara O'Shea said he is "proud" of how he and his team-mates came through a trying October international window.

During a four-game Nations League schedule, Heimir Hallgrimsson's side lost away to Kosovo and drew at home to Austria - who they are preparing to face in return fixtures - but it was two games against Israel which tested their resolve.

O'Shea stepped in as captain in the absence of injured skipper Nathan Collins and the 27-year-old acknowledged it "was a tough situation to be in" as they faced Israel in two games on neutral territory.

The first of those resulted in a 3-0 victory for the Irish in Hungary, a game that looked in doubt the previous day when training was delayed as players took a vote on whether to play - amid protests over the Israel-Gaza war - with goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu making himself unavailable for selection.

The sides drew 1-1 in the second meeting in Serbia and, while the saga proved a challenge for all within the Republic of Ireland squad, O'Shea - who missed the second game for personal reasons - paid tribute to his team-mates for the support he received as stand-in skipper.

"I think I was quite lucky, I am really proud to be part of the group, with some great people in it," said the Ipswich Town captain.

"Even the players playing now as well, they are great leaders themselves. I never felt I was fully alone in having to do anything

"There were always people around me. I always keep level-headed, I don't get too high with the highs or too low with the lows."

He added: "Of course it was a difficult time, it was a time that I had to learn stuff about myself, how I was going to react to things. But I think as a group we did excellently.

"It was a tough situation to be in, but we overcame it as best we could. And I am really proud of the group and the staff."

Seamus Coleman has been without a club since leaving Everton at the end of last season

Collins is back to lead the team for Saturday's trip to face Austria in Linz and the final League B3 game at home to Kosovo on Tuesday (both 19:45 GMT).

Also part of the squad is Seamus Coleman, who has taken on a 'hybrid role' despite not being named in manager Hallgrimsson's official 24-man squad.

"It's great to have them [Collins and Coleman] back," O'Shea continued.

"It would have been great if they were there in the last camp as well, but we had some really good people in that last camp who were doing great things.

"Nathan's the captain, so it's always great to have him back in. Seamus' knowledge is so, so valuable to us. I think we are a stronger group when we have them two with us."

Coleman has been without a club since leaving Everton at the end of last season, following 17 years with the Toffees.

The 38-year-old defender recently said he is considering retirement but Republic of Ireland assistant coach John O'Shea is delighted to have the Donegal man around the squad.

"It's us helping Seamus and Seamus helping us," O'Shea said of Coleman's role on the training pitch.

"To see the impact he's having, the quality that remains in his ability and the driving and pushing he's doing for everyone in the group has been good to see. Not much has changed."

The severity and nature of the threat against Scott Bessent remains unclear

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has been moved from his Washington DC home to a military base after Iran-linked threats to his life, according to US media reports.

CBS, the BBC's US partner, said the relocation came after a photo of Bessent's home was published in the Wall Street Journal.

Bessent has been at the forefront of efforts to isolate Iran economically through sanctions and a wider economic blockade.

While the exact nature of the threats against Bessent remain unclear, US intelligence has warned that Iran has "substantially increased" efforts to target Americans, including US officials.

"After the Wall Street Journal published an article featuring an online photo that allowed the location of the secretary's Georgetown home to be geo-located, security concerns began to increase," a source told CBS.

Georgetown is an affluent part of Washington that is home to a number of government officials and prominent residents.

Those security concerns, the source added, prompted authorities to move Bessent to a military base in the area.

In a statement, a Treasury Department spokesperson said only that Bessent "will not be deterred" by threats and "remains committed" to the US effort to pressure Iran's economy.

The BBC has contacted the White House for comment.

In September, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warned that Iran has "substantially increased" efforts to target Americans.

The New York Times has reported that the Iranian effort includes the targeting of current and former US officials. One source told the newspaper this has "reached a more advanced stage".

Other US officials reportedly on Iran's list of potential targets include former Secretary of State Mike Pompeo, former National Security Advisor John Bolton and Mark Milley, the former chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff.

Milley and Bolton's security teams were taken away by the Trump administration shortly after he returned to office last year.

Bessent is one of a number of administration officials that live on military bases. The White House's new chief of staff, Stephen Miller, was moved to a base in late 2025 - before the conflict with Iran began.

Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth and Secretary of State Marco Rubio both live on military bases, as did former Attorney General Pam Bondi and former intelligence chief Tulsi Gabbard.

The US and Israel launched an air campaign against Iran in February, killing its leader and prompting the regime in Tehran to retaliate with strikes on US allies across the region and the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, through which around a fifth of the world's oil and gas usually travels.

In June, the US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated a blockade targeting Iranian ports.

MN202611_nqir2faoh1.t:
Harry Kane was given a special shirt by Prince William and Peter Shilton before kick-off

"It's great when fairytales come true," England boss Roy Hodgson said after 21-year-old Tottenham striker Harry Kane scored 79 seconds into his international debut back in 2015.

"Let's hope it's the start of a good and long England career for him."

Eleven years on, Kane made his 126th appearance for his country and became the most-capped men's player in Three Lions history when England played Croatia in the Nations League at Wembley on Thursday.

His record-extending 92nd England goal came from the spot in their 2-1 win.

Peter Shilton, who served England as a goalkeeper, won 125 caps between 1970 and 1990.

Shilton was part of a presentation to Kane with a special framed England shirt before kick-off.

"It's not about me - it's about the team," said Kane beforehand.

"I love coming to every England camp, I love playing every game and representing the country in the best way possible."

Kane, 33, has gone through every emotion playing for his country.

He fought back tears after missing a penalty in the World Cup quarter-final defeat by France in 2022, and sang Wonderwall with fans following the win over Croatia at this summer's World Cup - which he labelled one of his "favourite ever moments" in a Three Lions shirt.

London-born Kane is the boy who grew up in Chingford to captain his country, become England's record goalscorer and win the 2026 Ballon d'Or.

Now the Bayern Munich striker has made more appearances than any other man in England's football history.

"He wins the Ballon d'Or, and deservedly so, and in the next game for England he gets the all-time record with 126 matches," England boss Thomas Tuchel said about Kane when announcing his squad last week.

"Thursday is a deserved occasion to celebrate an extraordinary player."

Long before Kane made his first senior appearance for his country in a 4-0 Euro 2016 qualifying win over Lithuania at Wembley, he was an England fan.

Aged 12, he remembers the heartache of going out on penalties to Portugal in the quarter-finals of the 2006 World Cup under Sven-Goran Eriksson and failing to qualify for Euro 2008 under Steve McClaren.

"During most major tournaments we would go to the pub to watch England, with the beer garden and the screen," said Kane.

"We loved England, we loved watching England and we were big England fans. I remember many tears being shed after we went out on penalties and things like that."

Kane fell in love with football from an early age.

Aged five, he wrote about his ambition to become a footballer in a school project.

Weekends and holidays were spent playing football in his local Ridgeway Park with his dad Patrick and brother Charlie.

They would use trees as goalposts, with the two brothers taking turns to shoot while Patrick was in goal.

At the age of five, Kane wrote "I want to play football" in a school project

At Larkswood Primary School, Kane and his friends would play football in the playground - where they were only allowed to use tennis balls.

By then, the future England captain was playing for Sunday league team Ridgeway Rovers - whose former players included David Beckham, Kane's idol growing up.

Former Manchester United midfielder Beckham, who won 115 England caps between 1996 and 2009, was playing for Real Madrid when Kane was at Chingford Foundation School.

"He had sent a Real Madrid shirt back to our secondary school," added Kane.

"Seeing Beckham's shirt hanging there growing up and knowing he grew up in the same surroundings as I did was a source of great motivation."

2015: Celebrating his first goal on his senior England debut against Lithuania aged 21

2017: First game as England captain - a 2-2 World Cup qualifying draw against Scotland at Hampden Park

2018: First England hat-trick against Panama at the 2018 World Cup in Russia

2023: Celebrating becoming England men's record goalscorer after scoring against Italy in a Euro 2024 qualifier in Naples

2024: Receiving a 'golden' cap to mark his 100th England appearance in a Nations League game against Finland at Wembley

Wayne Rooney was England captain and Joe Hart was goalkeeper when Kane came on to make his Three Lions debut 11 years ago.

"My reaction when he first came into the England squad was: 'Alright, who is this guy?'" Hart told BBC Sport of the young Tottenham striker called up after scoring 26 goals in 42 league and cup games in 2014-15.

"Then I was like: 'Oh OK, he's good! Then he kept coming back [into the England squad] and my reaction was: 'Flipping heck, he's getting better!'

"I went to Tottenham during Covid and it got to the point in training where he was that good that I wasn't even diving for his shots. I was thinking: 'I adore you, but you are frustrating the life out of me.'"

Kane has served five different England managers.

As well as Hodgson and current boss Tuchel, Kane won 81 of his 125 caps under Gareth Southgate, played for Lee Carsley when he was interim boss in 2024, and appeared in Sam Allardyce's sole match in charge in 2016.

It was Southgate who recognised Kane's leadership skills and handed him the England captaincy for the first time in 2017, even though Kane was not captain of Tottenham at the time.

"I want people with leadership qualities who are respected by the group, and capable of stepping forward at the right moments and handling responsibility," said Southgate.

When he has started, Kane has captained the Three Lions 97 times - more than anyone else.

"Amazing" Kane targets 100 international goals

How long will Kane carry on playing for England? More worryingly, who will lead the attack when he retires?

Despite individual awards and back-to-back Bundesliga titles with Bayern Munich, Kane has yet to inspire his country to a major trophy.

He will be approaching 35 when England, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland co-host Euro 2028.

"He aged, but he got better too, like red wine," Lothar Matthaus, West Germany's 1990 World Cup-winning captain, told BBC Sport.

Kane, who has had to adapt his game to stay at the top level, is certainly not ready to talk publicly about retirement dates while he is still only 33.

"From a physical point of view, I feel great," he told BBC Sport recently.

"My numbers are as high as ever, and I've recently reached a new top speed in a game against Borussia Dortmund. I'm going to keep pushing and see what else is possible."

A Madame Tussauds figure of Harry Kane with Peter Shilton and players from Ridgeway Rovers - the club Kane played for as a boy

Kane's former Tottenham and England team-mate Hart added: "He's never particularly relied on pace. It's all about his thought process and his brain and how he calculates the game."

The Three Lions have won 84, drawn 22 and lost 20 of his 126 games.

His 92 goals for his country include 59 with his right foot, 15 with the left and 18 headers, with three from outside the box. Twenty-seven have come from the penalty spot.

"I'm speechless" - Kane reacts to England's victory over Mexico

Kane's rise from Leyton Orient loan signing to Ballon d'Or winner is well-documented.

His story - the model student and family man who married his childhood sweetheart and became an England great - serves as a reminder to pupils at his old school to never give up on their dreams.

He has not forgotten his roots - or the clubs that helped him on his pathway.

In 2020, Kane sponsored Leyton Orient's shirt. The club's home strip carried a message of thanks to frontline workers tackling the coronavirus pandemic.

Mental health charity Mind and Haven House Children's Hospice also had their logos on Orient's two change shirts as part of the deal.

"I was born and brought up only a couple of miles from Orient's stadium and I'm really happy to have the opportunity to give back to the club that gave me my first professional start," said Kane at the time.

"It also gives me a platform to say a big thank you to the many frontline heroes and charities out there who provide care and support during these challenging times."

Matthaus, who has witnessed Kane's impact at Bayern Munich, added: "He is a good person, a good ambassador, the captain of the English national team playing at a German club."

On Thursday, England's players and fans saluted Kane for breaking another record and making it 126 not out.
